Let us speak plainly about the moral calculus.

On one side: A patient whose impaired refusal is overridden. They wake up alive. They may be angry. They may file a complaint. They may feel violated—and that feeling is real and must be addressed with compassion and accountability.

On the other side: A patient who dies. Their family grieves forever. Their children grow up without a parent. Their potential—every future choice, every future autonomous act they would ever make—is extinguished. Permanently. Irreversibly.

Death is the ultimate violation of autonomy. A dead person has no autonomy. No choices. No future preferences. No ability to change their mind.

If we truly value autonomy—not as an abstract principle but as a lived human capacity—then we must recognize that keeping a person alive is the precondition for all autonomy that follows. You cannot respect a dead person's future wishes. You cannot give choices to someone in a grave.

The asymmetry is overwhelming. Override and save: the patient lives to object, to sue, to advocate, to tell their story, to make future autonomous choices. Honor the refusal and lose: silence. Forever.

We already commit individuals who are a danger to themselves due to mental health crises. We restrain patients who, in delirium, try to pull out their own endotracheal tubes. We treat unconscious patients under implied consent precisely because we assume they would want to live. We mandate treatment for minors over parental religious objections because we recognize that some decisions are too consequential to leave to compromised judgment.

We already believe, in a hundred different contexts, that the preservation of life justifies temporary limitation of expressed preference when capacity is in question.

I am simply asking us to be consistent. I am asking us to extend to the hemorrhaging accident victim the same presumption we extend to the unconscious one—the presumption of the will to live.

To the Medical Professionals in This Room

To the doctors and nurses listening: I know what I am asking. I know the weight of it.

You chose this profession because something in you answered a call—a call to fight death, to ease suffering, to stand between a human being and oblivion. Every day, you make impossible decisions under impossible pressure with impossible stakes.

I am not asking you to play God. I am asking that we stop forcing you to play spectator when you have the power to save a life.

You should not have to stand at that bedside—with the tools in your hands and the knowledge in your mind and the oath in your heart—and do nothing because a system designed for the calm of the courtroom has been imposed on the chaos of the trauma bay.

You deserve a framework that trusts your judgment. That recognizes your training. That acknowledges that you—not the lawyer, not the ethicist sitting comfortably at a desk the next morning, not the judge reading the chart months later—you are the one who must live with the outcome.

When that young mother's children ask why their mother died—when they are old enough to understand that she was in a hospital, surrounded by people who could have saved her, who had the blood and the skill and the time—what do we tell them?

Do we tell them about autonomy? Do we explain Kantian ethics to a nine-year-old? Do we describe the philosophical beauty of self-determination to children who will never again feel their mother's arms around them?

Or do we tell them the truth: that we had the power to save her, and we chose—we chose—a legal and ethical framework that valued a confused utterance over a human life?

I say we must do better. I say we must build a system brave enough to say: In the emergency, when the mind is compromised and the body is failing, we choose life. We choose to give that patient the chance to wake up, to recover, to exercise true autonomy with a functioning brain and a beating heart.

We choose life, and we let the patient thank us—or curse us—in the morning.

Because in the morning, they will be alive to do either one.

And that—that—is what it means to truly serve the sacred duty of medicine.
